title: With populations shrinking, does property still have a future in Malaysia?
shortTitle: Is there a future for property?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #218 | IS THERE FUTURE FOR MALAYSIA REAL ESTATE?
excerpt: A viewer asks whether falling birth rates and crashes in China and Hong Kong mean property is a bad bet. Sean explains why he still backs Malaysian property, and where demand will move.

qa.asker: N, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: N notes that people mock property investors as markets fall in places such as China and Hong Kong, and that Japan, South Korea and Taiwan have shrinking populations with little immigration. N worries that unaffordable prices will mean fewer families, fewer buyers and more empty homes, so that supply outruns demand and prices fall further.
qa.question: Should people still be encouraged to own property, and will falling populations eventually crash prices?
qa.quote: In Malaysia property is still the way to go.
qa.answer: In Malaysia, yes. The country still has a large young workforce, the government leans on construction and new highways to grow the economy, and buyers here need far less upfront than elsewhere. Smaller families will change what people want, towards smaller homes in convenient city locations, but prime areas will stay out of reach to buy and become places people rent.

reasons.title: Other markets work differently
reasons.body: Hong Kong develops only about a quarter of its land, and in China buyers own development rights rather than land and pay large upfront sums, while towns are often built before the jobs arrive. Their troubles don't translate directly to Malaysia.

reasons.title: Demand follows jobs
reasons.body: Most people still have to be near their workplace, so city locations keep their value while big suburban homes become less relevant over generations. Smaller families favour two-bedroom units in convenient places over large landed homes far out.

reasons.title: Prime areas become rent-only
reasons.body: Owning a landed home in places like Bangsar is already beyond most young buyers, and the wealthy keep buying assets that grow. In future, Sean expects the bragging point to be where you rent, not what you own.

reasons.title: Malaysia still offers openings
reasons.body: Most countries require about 25% down, while Malaysia asks 10% or less, and foreigners increasingly see it as a place to retire. Sean also sees value in Johor Bahru now that its price bubble has burst.

actions: Separate homes from investments: buy homes for comfort, and investments where jobs and transport create rental demand.
Judge each location on its own data rather than nationwide headlines about oversupply or crashes.
Expect demand to favour smaller, well-connected units as households shrink.
In expensive prime areas, compare the rent with the price; renting there can be excellent value.
Keep making informed decisions and taking calculated risks rather than rushing in or staying out on fear.
qa.caveat: Sean says he can't speak for markets outside Malaysia, and the shift away from large suburban homes he describes plays out over decades, not years.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #218. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Views are Sean's as of August 2023.
